overview.body:
**Daidalos** ​(*daedalus*) — ‌Craftsman, Inventor, ‌Wings · ​Cunningly ​wrought — ​belongs to ​the Greek ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Craftsman, ​Inventor, ‌Wings". The ​name means ‌"Cunningly wrought"[^1].

​**Daidalos** ​is the ​master craftsman ​of Greek ​mythology: ‌the architect ​of the ‌Labyrinth, the ​maker ‌of moving ​statues, and ‌the father ​of ‌Icarus. His ​name means ​"cunningly wrought" ‌and became ‌a ‌byword for ​any work ​so skillful ‌that ​it seemed ​alive. He ‌is the ​first ​engineer in ‌Western literature, ​the inventor ‌whose ​ingenuity saves ​him and ​destroys those ​he ‌loves.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as ‌**Daidalos** ​and serves ​its temple ‌at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/daedalus/). The ‌original ‌carries both ​stress and ‌vowel length, ​and ​exactly one ​historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*daedalus* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Δαίδαλος**. Etymologically ​it ​means ​"Cunningly wrought"[^1].

‌The ​ASCII form ​*daedalus* ‌survives only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ​it ​is a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Daidalos** ‌recovers ​the full ‌diacritic ​detail of ​the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. ‌The original ​carries ​both stress ‌and ​vowel length, ​and ‌exactly one ​historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration ​exists, which ​places ​the name ‌in ‌Tier ​1.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- ‌**d** → ‌**D** ‌— Same
‌- ​**a** → ‌**a** ​— Same
​- ​**e** → ‌**i** ​— ​Iota
- ​**d** ‌→ **d** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ‌Same
- ​**l** ‌→ **l** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**u** ​→ ​**o** — ​Omicron
​- **s** ‌→ ‌**s** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/dai̯.da.los/** ​— Attic ​Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Dai-** ​— Long ​diphthong αι ‌[ai̯] with ​acute ‌pitch accent; ​the alpha ‌is open ​and the ​iota ​forms an ​off-glide.
- ​**-da-** — ‌Short ​[da], the ‌middle syllable ​of the ‌name.
​- **-los** ‌— Short ​[los], the ‌final syllable ​with ​a clear ‌liquid l.

‌For the ‌modern ​speaker, the ​closest approximation ‌is: 'DIE-dah-los' ​— the ​first ‌syllable is ​long and ​carries the ‌ancient ​pitch rise; ‌the remaining ​syllables are ​short ​and light.

​Kindred and ‌historical forms ‌of the ​name:

‌- **Greek** ​— Δαίδαλος ​(Daidalos), the ‌cunningly ‌wrought craftsman
‌- **Latin** ‌— Daedalus, ​the Roman ‌rendering ​adopted into ​English

The ​Greek Δαίδαλος ‌contains ​both stress ​(acute on ​the diphthong) ‌and ​length (the ​diphthong αι ​is long), ‌making it ​a ‌Tier 1 ​restoration. The ‌Latin-derived English ​form ‌Daedalus is ‌a secondary ​spelling that ​preserves the ​consonants ​but obscures ‌the original ‌Greek vowel ​quantities.

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is written ‌in ​Greek ​as ​**Δαίδαλος**. ​This original ​script ‌is ​the ​form against ‌which ​the ‌ASCII ​fallback *daedalus* ‌and ​the ​PuniCodex ​restoration ​**Daidalos** are ​measured: ‌the ​restoration ‌preserves its ​full ‌diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the written ‌form, ​so ​that ‌a reader ‌typing ‌the ​modern ​address still ‌speaks ​the ​ancient ‌name.[^1]

​The name ​is ‌written ​in ‌Greek as ​**Δαίδαλος**. ​The ​first ​syllable ‌is a ‌long ​diphthong ‌αι ​with an ​acute ‌accent. ‌The ‌plain ASCII ‌*daedalus* ​flattens ‌the ​diphthong ​into ae ​and ‌removes ​the ​accent. The ​PuniCodex ‌restoration ​**Daidalos** ​preserves ​the scholarly ‌transliteration ​of ‌the ​Greek form ‌and ​is ‌classified ‌as Tier ​1 ​because ​the ​diphthong ‌is long ‌and ​accented.

domains.body:
**Daidalos** ​is ‌the master ‌craftsman ​of ​Greek mythology: ​the ​architect ​of the ‌Labyrinth, ​the ​maker of ‌moving ​statues, ‌and the ​father ‌of ​Icarus. His ​name ​means ​"cunningly wrought" ​and ‌became ​a ‌byword for ​any ‌work ​so skillful ‌that ​it ‌seemed alive. ​He ​is ‌the first ‌engineer ‌in ​Western literature, ​the ‌inventor ​whose ingenuity ​saves ‌him ​and destroys ​those ‌he ​loves.[^1]

‌### The ​Labyrinth

​The ​maze Daidalos ​built ‌to ‌contain the ​Minotaur ‌at ​Knossos.

### ​Wings

‌The ‌feathered wings ‌he ‌fashioned ​from wax ‌and ​twine ​to escape ​Crete.

‌### ​Automata

​The moving ​statues ‌he ​made so ​lifelike ​that ‌they had ​to ‌be ​chained down.

‌### ​Invention

‌The transforming ‌power ​of ​human skill, ​celebrated ​and ‌feared by ‌the ​Greeks.

mythology.body:
The myths ​of Daidalos are ‌preserved in Homer, ‌the lost *Catalogue ​of Women*, Diodorus ​Siculus, Ovid, ​and Apollodorus. They ​celebrate the power ​of human invention ‌and warn against ​its costs: jealousy, ​exile, and the ‌death of a ​son.[^1]

### The ‌Killing of Talos ​(Athens)

Daidalos was ‌born in ​Athens, where his ​skill as an ​inventor aroused the ​jealousy of his ​nephew Talos (or ‌Perdix). When the ​boy invented the ‌saw and the ​potter's wheel, Daidalos ‌threw him from ​the Acropolis ‌in envy. For ​this murder he ‌was exiled from ​Athens and fled ​to Crete, where ‌King Minos welcomed ‌him.[^2]

### The ‌Labyrinth (Crete)

At ​Knossos, Daidalos built ​the Labyrinth to ‌house the ​Minotaur, the half-man, ​half-bull born of ‌Pasiphae. The maze ​was so cunningly ​designed that even ‌its maker could ​barely find his ‌way out. When ​Theseus came to ​slay the Minotaur, ​Ariadne gave ​him the thread ‌that Daidalos had ‌taught her to ​use.

### The ‌Wings (Crete)

When ​Minos imprisoned Daidalos ​and his son ‌Icarus in the ‌Labyrinth, Daidalos made ‌wings from feathers ‌and wax. ​He warned Icarus ‌not to fly ​too close to ​the sun, but ​the boy, exulting ‌in flight, ignored ​him. The wax ​melted, Icarus fell ​into the sea, ‌and Daidalos flew ​on alone ​to Sicily.

### ​Death of Daidalos ‌(Sicily)

In Sicily, ​Daidalos built marvellous ‌works for King ​Cocalus. When Minos ‌came to demand ​his surrender, Cocalus' ‌daughters killed Minos ‌in his bath. ​Daidalos lived ​out his life ​in Sicily, still ​inventing, still exiled ‌from the ordinary ‌happiness of family ​and home.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Daidalos ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Greek ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Δαίδαλος, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​craftsman ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(wings ​and ​wax). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sources.citation: Morris, Sarah, Daidalos and the Origins of Greek Art (1992).

meditation.body:
Daidalos ​is ‌the ‌first ​Western portrait ​of ​the ​inventor ​as ‌tragic ​hero. ​His gifts ‌are ​extraordinary; ‌his ​judgement ‌is ​not. ​He kills ​his ​nephew ​from ‌envy, ​builds ‌a ​prison ‌for a ​monster, ‌and ​loses ‌his ​son ​to ‌the very ‌technology ‌that ​saved ​him. ‌Each ​invention ​solves one ‌problem ​and ​creates ‌another.

​To ‌meditate ​on ​Daidalos is ​to ​meditate ‌on ‌the ​double ‌edge ​of human ​making. ‌We ‌are ‌the ‌species ​that ‌makes wings, ​and ​we ​are ‌the ​species ​whose ​children ‌fly too ​high. ​The ​question ‌is ​not ‌whether ​to invent ‌but ​whether ‌we ‌can ​invent ​with ​the humility ​that ‌knows ‌our ​limits.[^1]
